**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 2 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section » (5 en tout, au moins 2 par section). `regles_choix` ne sait exprimer que « n parmi m » : chaque section porte la règle minimale (2 sur 4) ; la règle « 5 en tout » n'est pas exprimable et figure dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : le sujet imprime les points de chaque partie (a) et (b), jamais le total de la question ; `points` de l'exercice est donc laissé vide. Les parties totalisent 20 pour chaque question (10+10, 10+10, 10+10, 10+10, 12+8, 12+8, 12+8, 8+12), conformément à « All questions carry equal marks ». Aucun écart constaté.

Sujet scanné (filigrane gcerevision.com en travers de la page ; sur la page de garde, le texte du verso apparaît en transparence, en miroir) : l'ensemble reste lisible. Titre, niveau (ADVANCED LEVEL), code 0725, session JUNE 2026 et durée (trois heures) vérifiés sur la page de garde. Le sujet ne compte que deux pages : page de garde, puis les huit questions (Section A : 1 à 4 ; Section B : 5 à 8) sur une seule page.

Défaut d'impression : à la question 5(b) la lettre « (b) » est maculée (« (ḅ) ») ; lue comme (b) d'après la séquence (a), (b). Le numéro « 2 » en en-tête de page de garde est imprimé de façon approximative (« Economics 2 »).

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont rédigés (niveau Advanced). Les exemples chiffrés (TVA au taux hypothétique de 20 %, chaîne cacao 100 000 / 160 000 / 250 000 / 320 000 FCFA, élasticité de -0,5) sont hypothétiques et recalculés avec Python ; le taux de 20 % n'est pas le taux légal camerounais. Aucune statistique réelle n'est avancée.

Figures : trois schémas produits avec matplotlib (Q2 fig-1 prix agricoles à demande inélastique, Q2 fig-2 stock régulateur, Q6 fig-1 encaisses d'activité et de spéculation). Ils illustrent les corrigés ; le sujet n'imprime aucune figure. Les courbes sont schématiques, sans échelle chiffrée.
Question 6(a) : « diagram(s) » demandé par le sujet ; le diagramme est décrit dans le corrigé et fourni en figure (Keynes : L1 fonction du revenu, L2 fonction du taux d'intérêt, trappe à liquidité).

questions.enonce_markdown: How can efficiency of labour be improved in an economy? (10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The **efficiency (productivity) of labour** is the output produced per worker, or per hour worked, in a given period: $\text{labour productivity} = \dfrac{\text{total output}}{\text{number of workers (or hours)}}$. Higher efficiency means more output from the same labour input, so lower unit costs, higher wages and faster economic growth. It can be improved through the following measures.

1. **Education and training.** Formal education, vocational and technical training, apprenticeships and on-the-job training give workers more skills and knowledge (**human capital**). Skilled workers make fewer mistakes, learn new techniques faster and adapt to new technology.
2. **Better health, nutrition and living conditions.** Healthy and well-fed workers have more energy, fewer days of absence and longer working lives. Health care, clean water, safe housing and disease control (for example against malaria) raise efficiency.
3. **Division of labour and specialisation.** When each worker concentrates on one task, he or she becomes more skilled, time is not lost moving between jobs and machines can be used for repetitive tasks. Its limits are boredom, dependence on other workers and the size of the market.
4. **More and better capital.** Workers using machines, tools, fertilisers or computers produce more than workers using only their hands. Capital deepening (more capital per worker) and technical progress raise output per worker.
5. **Incentives and motivation.** Higher real wages, performance-related pay, bonuses, profit-sharing, promotion prospects and job security encourage workers to put in more effort. Good working conditions and good relations between employers and workers also raise morale.
6. **Good management and organisation.** Skilled managers plan production, match workers to jobs, supervise, reduce waste and avoid idle time.
7. **Improved infrastructure.** Reliable electricity, roads, telecommunications and water supply reduce delays and breakdowns, so that workers can use their time productively (for example, power cuts in Douala or Yaounde cost firms working hours).
8. **Better placement of labour.** Employment exchanges, labour market information and better mobility help workers to find the jobs for which they are best suited, so that talent is not wasted.
9. **Government policy.** Public spending on schools and hospitals, subsidies for training, a stable macroeconomic environment, and laws on safety and working hours all help.

**Evaluation.** Education and training raise productivity only after a long time lag and are costly, and higher efficiency can cause short-term unemployment if firms produce the same output with fewer workers. The best results come from combining training, capital, incentives and good management, rather than relying on one measure.

**Conclusion.** The efficiency of labour is improved mainly by raising the skill, health and motivation of workers, by giving them more and better capital to work with, and by good organisation and a supportive environment.

questions.enonce_markdown: In what ways can the government improve on geographical mobility of labour? (10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** **Geographical mobility of labour** is the ability and willingness of workers to move from one place (region, town or country) to another in search of work or better pay. It is often low because of obstacles such as high costs of moving, shortage of housing in the destination, family and social ties, lack of information, and poor transport. The government can reduce these obstacles in the following ways.

1. **Provision of housing.** Building low-cost public housing in growing towns, regulating rents and encouraging private house-building reduce the biggest barrier, the shortage and high price of accommodation in areas with jobs.
2. **Removal (relocation) grants and allowances.** Paying part of the cost of transporting a worker's family and belongings, or giving a transfer allowance to civil servants posted to another region, lowers the cost of moving. Tax relief on moving expenses has a similar effect.
3. **Improved transport and communications.** Better roads, railways and public transport make it easier to move or to commute, and good telephone and internet networks keep families in touch, reducing the feeling of isolation.
4. **Information on jobs.** Public employment services and employment exchanges, job centres, radio and web-based notices about vacancies in different regions remove ignorance about opportunities elsewhere.
5. **Regional (decentralisation) policy.** Taking jobs to workers, through industrial estates, tax holidays and public investment in less-developed regions, reduces the need to move; at the same time, providing schools, hospitals, water and electricity in the destination areas makes them attractive to migrants.
6. **Removing legal and institutional barriers.** Simplifying land-tenure rules (so that a migrant can buy or rent land), recognising professional qualifications across the country, removing local restrictions on settlement and ensuring that pension and social-security rights are transferable make movement easier. Within regional integration schemes such as CEMAC, free-movement agreements and common documents facilitate cross-border mobility.
7. **Security and law and order.** Guaranteeing safety in towns and growing regions removes fear that discourages workers from moving.
8. **Training and education programmes.** Training workers in skills required in other regions raises their ability to move (this also improves occupational mobility).
9. **Wage and benefit policy.** Paying public-sector workers extra for work in remote or less-attractive regions (hardship allowances) encourages them to relocate there.

**Evaluation.** Such measures are costly for the government, may take a long time to work and may cause problems of their own: rural-urban drift can create overcrowding and unemployment in cities and depopulate villages. The government must therefore balance mobility with the development of rural areas.

**Conclusion.** The government can raise geographical mobility mainly by lowering the costs of moving, improving housing, transport and information, and developing the regions, so that labour can move to where it is most productive.
